blocks.text: Shree Refrigerations Limited (SRL) designs, manufactures, installs and services marine-grade air-conditioning, refrigeration and HVAC systems for Indian Navy warships and submarines, defence PSUs and shipyards, from a single manufacturing base at Karad, Satara district, Maharashtra [F] (AR2026 p.40). The product set is narrow and specified: AC plants (5 TR to 300 TR, seawater- or air-cooled), refrigeration plants (0.5 TR to 35 TR), turnkey HVAC&R packages, marinised split and self-contained air conditioners, AHU/ATU and fan-coil units, and electrical starter and control panels [F] (PPT Aug 2026). **Defence contributed 95% of FY26 business** [F] (AR2026 p.12).

Revenue arrives through four streams: equipment supply for new-build ships and for retrofits of ships in refit; installation and commissioning; spares (onboard spares supplied with the equipment, and base-and-depot spares replenished on roughly two- and five-year cycles); and AMC/life-cycle services [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Orders are won almost entirely through shipyard and Navy tenders on a lowest-bidder basis, and contracts are predominantly fixed-price with no price-adjustment clause [F] (RATING); [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

FY26 consolidated revenue from operations was Rs 153.55 cr against Rs 98.73 cr in FY25, up 55.5%, with consolidated PAT of Rs 21.53 cr and standalone PAT of Rs 21.40 cr [F] (AR2026 p.24). Reported EPS was Rs 6.47 basic / Rs 6.35 diluted standalone [F] (AR2026 p.38). Our statements data shows the same shape: sales Rs 154 cr, EBITDA Rs 33 cr, operating margin 21%, PAT Rs 22 cr [F] (NUMBERS).

subsections.title: Listing status and what it does to the evidence base

blocks.text: SRL listed on the **SME platform of BSE on 1 August 2025** through an IPO of 93,86,000 shares at Rs 125 - a fresh issue of Rs 94.51 cr and an offer for sale of Rs 22.81 cr - which was subscribed 187 times [F] (AR2026 p.11, p.33). It has been a listed company for roughly thirteen months and has published exactly one annual report and two post-earnings calls.

items: Because it is on the SME platform, the company is exempt from the detailed corporate-governance disclosures of Regulation 15 of SEBI LODR and has not published a corporate governance report [F] (AR2026 p.28-29).

It reports half-yearly, not quarterly, and management has explicitly defended that choice: 'in our line of business, it might indicate incorrect conclusions to you... a half yearly or actually even an annual reporting is more accurate than a quarterly reporting' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Two separate investors asked for quarterly updates on that call [F] (CALL Jun 2026).
As a result, on today's date the most recent reported financials are for the year ended 31 March 2026 - close to six months stale - for a company guiding to 40% compound growth [AI].
Management stated it is not permitted to migrate to the main board 'for another two years at least' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

There is no history of listed-company disclosure to test management against: the FY26 annual report is the first, the prior period comparatives are unlisted-company numbers, and our statements data carries only six years of annual history rather than ten [F] (NUMBERS).
Institutional participation is negligible - FII 0.12% and DII 8.74% at March 2026, across 4,461 shareholders [F] (NUMBERS).

rows: A 200-day reduction in one year proves a structural fix and de-risks the growth plan

The AONs are government approvals-in-principle, not tenders and not orders; management itself says they 'will translate into orders over the next two years' and that ~Rs 1,000 cr of tenders will be floated, with the win rate undetermined [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Genuinely unresolved - and it is the single most important number to watch at the H1 FY27 result [AI]

blocks.text: The market appears to be underwriting SRL as a defence-indigenisation compounder: a monopoly-adjacent supplier with a 40% growth runway, riding an order cycle that has barely begun. The evidence supports something narrower and more fragile. SRL is a genuinely differentiated, genuinely qualified naval HVAC sub-contractor - the three-directorate registration and the type-tested product range are real and are not purchasable - but it sells fixed-price, tender-won, lowest-bidder contracts into three or four shipyard customers, with no escalation clause, no pricing power, no disclosed concentration, and a working-capital cycle that consumes cash faster than profit creates it. Its order book shrank 17% in the half year in which its revenue doubled; its highest-margin revenue line collapsed from 30% of sales to 7% and represents at most 6.6% of the forward book; its Section 198 profits were declared 'inadequate' to support the family's remuneration in the same year it reported record PAT; and the corporate vehicle carrying the data-centre narrative has no revenue at all. **The variant view is not that the business is bad - it is that a high-quality niche engineering business with sub-investment-grade credit and negative cumulative operating cash flow is being priced as though it were a structural compounder, and that the gap between Rs 375 and even the most generous DCF output of Rs 106.9 is too large to be closed by any plausible improvement in the operating story** [AI]; [F] (NUMBERS).

**Three of the five board changes in FY26 were promoter-family appointments or re-appointments** (Rajashri Shende, Rucha Shende) [F] (AR2026 p.25), made in a single board meeting on 23 February 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.26).

The company was a private limited company until 2024 and a listed company only from August 2025 - so the FY26 annual report is both the first and the only listed-company report available for testing management's claims [AI].

sections.title: The production chain and where value is captured

items: **1. Tender and bid.** A shipyard or the Navy floats a tender for an AC plant, refrigeration plant, turnkey HVAC package or control panel on a named platform. Award is to the lowest qualifying bidder from the relevant directorate's vendor list [F] (RATING). Tender fees rose from Rs 0.01 cr to Rs 0.58 cr in FY26, consistent with a much higher bid volume [F] (AR2026 p.49).

**2. Design and design approval.** SRL's in-house design office - management cites 21 people in design - adapts the product to the platform; the design must be approved by the relevant naval directorate before manufacture [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). For warship HVAC the company also co-develops with Knud E. Hansen, a Danish naval architecture firm [F] (AR2026 p.9).

**3. Type testing.** Each new capacity must be type tested to defence standards. Once a type is approved, repeat orders for the same product on other ships do not require re-testing [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Management states four of six Navy-standardised AC plant capacities, all six ATU capacities, all AFU capacities and about 70% of ventilation fan capacities are type tested [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). **This step is what made H1 FY26 revenue muted**: 'during the first half, we did all these type testing approvals, design approvals' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**4. Manufacture.** Fabrication, system assembly and finishing at Karad: CNC laser cutting, bending, drilling, special-purpose machines for tube sheets and condenser hole cutting, shot blasting, paint shop, robot welding, plate rolling, VMC/CNC and two 15T cranes on a 25m span [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

**5. Factory acceptance testing.** In-house rigs: a 300 TR chiller test bed with air-borne and structure-borne noise measurement, two 650 kW marine plant test beds, a controlled-ambient AC test room for HVAC/indoor units, climate-controlled testing for package ACs up to 15 TR, environmental chambers to 60 kW, refrigeration testing to -20 degC, a tilt test facility simulating ship motion (to 45 degrees for submarines), an AHU test bed of seven units, 40-channel data acquisition and leak-test facilities [F] (AR2026 p.14, p.15); [F] (PPT Aug 2026). 'Each stage advances only after formal inspection and approval by naval officials' [F] (AR2026 p.14).

**6. Delivery, installation and commissioning.** Executed on-site at the shipyard or dockyard by service teams based in Mumbai, Goa, Chennai, Vizag and Kolkata, with sales offices in Pune and Delhi and a Kochi office planned [F] (AR2026 p.14); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Management attributes part of the H1 FY26 margin fall to hiring 'large onsite manpower' for HVAC site execution [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

**7. Spares and life-cycle support.** Onboard spares supplied with the equipment (covering roughly a two-year requirement) and base-and-depot spares supplied mid-project (roughly a five-year requirement), plus AMC and preventive/corrective maintenance through the system life [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**8. Payment.** Multiple inspection and verification stages delay customer approvals, which is what blocks funds in receivables and inventory [F] (RATING). Advances received from customers rose from Rs 0.12 cr to Rs 9.48 cr in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.44).

subsections.title: Where value is captured - and where it leaks

blocks.text: Value is captured at exactly two points: the **approval position** (being on all three directorate vendor lists, with type-tested capacities, so that a repeat order needs no re-qualification) and the **single-point turnkey position** (as shipyards move from ordering AC, HVAC and panels separately to ordering a single turnkey package, a firm that makes all three does not need a partner) [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Management's own framing is explicit: 'Most of them produce one or the other. So, you are dependent upon somebody else to become your partner' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Value leaks at three points. **Price** - awards are to the lowest bidder on fixed-price contracts with no adjustment clause, so input inflation is borne by SRL [F] (RATING); [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). **Time** - execution runs two to three years per project, with customer-driven delivery dates management says it cannot accelerate: 'even if we want to... make H1 a blockbuster as much as H2, we may be constrained because the delivery period for a particular shipyard may actually lie in H2' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). **Cash** - multi-stage inspection and verification delays customer sign-off and therefore collection [F] (RATING). The result is a business with high stated margins and negative cumulative operating cash flow [E] (NUMBERS).

subsections.title: Overall read on the client base

blocks.text: The client base is high quality and low diversity. Every material customer is either a AAA-rated defence PSU shipyard or the Indian Navy itself, which removes credit risk almost entirely - and indeed the company carries a provision for doubtful debts of only Rs 0.35 cr against Rs 105.78 cr of gross receivables, 0.33% [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.47), with no disputed receivables at all [F] (AR2026 p.47). That is a legitimate defence of the receivable book: these debtors do not default, they just pay slowly [AI].

But the same fact caps the business. Three or four shipyard customers, one ultimate paymaster, tender-based award, fixed prices, no escalation clause and no long-term contracts mean SRL's revenue is a function of the Government of India's naval order calendar and of SRL's win rate within it - and nothing else [AI]. Stickiness is real at the platform level (a type-approved AC plant carries through a ship class and into spares) but weak at the customer level (each new class is a fresh tender, and management concedes 'as far as the newbuilds are concerned, that's the only place where we lost a few tenders') [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

The most important wallet-share question is unanswerable from disclosure: of the roughly Rs 271 cr order book, how much sits with each of GSL, HSL, MDL and GRSE, and how many of the eight ongoing projects come from a single shipyard? Management states four of the eight ongoing projects complete in FY27 [MC] (CALL Jun 2026) - if those four are concentrated with one customer, FY28 revenue visibility is far weaker than the headline order book implies [AI].

The company does disclose an order book, and it discloses it with a full-year movement - which is better practice than most SME-platform issuers [AI]. What it does not disclose is any L1 position, any tender-pipeline value in a published document, any customer-wise or platform-wise split of the book, or an execution schedule by period.

The evidence: total assets of Rs 294 cr support Rs 154 cr of revenue (0.52x asset turnover) while net fixed assets plus CWIP are only Rs 40 cr, or 14% of the balance sheet [E] from [F] (NUMBERS). subsections.title: Bottom line: is the margin improvement structural?

blocks.text: **There is no margin improvement to assess - there is a margin decline, and it is more structural than management presents it** [AI]. EBITDA margin has fallen in each of the last two years, from 31.0% in FY24 to 27.0% in FY25 to 21.0% in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS), and our statements data flags 'Margins compressing - operating margin 21% vs a 28% three-year average' as an amber item [F] (NUMBERS).

items: **Structural and permanent:** the fixed-cost base. Employee cost has risen from Rs 7.07 cr in FY23 to Rs 21.74 cr in FY26, from 14.0% to 14.2% of revenue - and management's own defence is forward-looking, not historical: 'Going forward, we look that new hiring will be at a very moderate level' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). That is an unfulfilled promise, not a fact [AI].

**Structural and adverse:** the contract form. Fixed-price, no escalation clause, two-to-three-year execution, in an acknowledged commodity upcycle [F] (RATING); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). This does not mean-revert on its own.

**Structural and favourable:** backward integration at Unit-2, which removes external partners from processes previously sub-contracted and should lift throughput [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Job work charges of Rs 2.35 cr are the visible target [F] (AR2026 p.48) - worth about 150 bp of margin if fully eliminated [E], though that is an upper bound and ignores the in-house cost of doing the work.

**Temporary and favourable:** the FY26 tax rate of 13.76%, unexplained and unlikely to persist at that level. Normalising to the FY25 rate of 30.4% would have cut FY26 PAT by roughly Rs 4.1 cr, from Rs 21.40 cr to about Rs 17.3 cr, and EPS from Rs 6.47 to about Rs 5.23 [E].

**Temporary and favourable, and about to reverse in the company's favour:** deferred revenue expenditure amortisation of Rs 2.98 cr a year is now fully written off - 'As of 31-03-2026, there is nil unamortised deferred revenue expenditure' [F] (AR2026 p.41). All else equal that adds roughly Rs 2.98 cr to FY27 pre-tax profit, about 12% of FY26 PBT [E] - offset by new depreciation on Unit-2 [AI].

**The swing factor:** spares mix. Management's entire margin-recovery case rests on spares returning to 15-20% of revenue [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). At most 6.6% of the closing order book is spares and services [E] from [F] (PPT Aug 2026). Until that changes, the recovery is an assertion.

blocks.text: Management's guided range of 20-24% EBITDA is below every year from FY21 to FY25 except FY23 [F] (NUMBERS). The guidance was also widened, not raised: 20-22% in November 2025 became 20-24% in May 2026 [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). **The company's own forward guidance concedes that the FY24 peak of 31% is not coming back** [AI].

sections.title: Unit economics - what can and cannot be built

blocks.text: **Unit economics cannot be built for this company from public disclosure.** The following inputs, each of which would be required, are all absent [F - absence of disclosure]:

items: **Volumes.** No units shipped, shipsets delivered by value, or tonnes processed are disclosed in any period. The presentation gives shipset counters (for example NGOPV 3 of 7) but attaches no rupee value to them [F] (PPT Aug 2026).
**Realisations.** No average selling price for an AC plant, HVAC package, refrigeration plant or control panel is disclosed anywhere.

**Capacity in output terms.** Capacity is stated in square feet, and in units per month for four products only - and for one of those four the annual report gives two figures differing by more than fivefold (10-15 versus up to 80 self-contained ACs per month) [F] (AR2026 p.14).
**Segment or product margins.** None. The company reports a single segment and treats AS 17 as inapplicable [F] (AR2026 p.41).

**Order-level economics.** Only one order value has ever been quantified: the P17A programme at 'around INR 150 crores' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), and the Rs 3.93 cr Navy order announced post year end [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS). Neither has a margin attached.
**Utilisation.** Not disclosed in any period.

subsections.title: What would have to be true for unit economics to improve

items: **Spares and services back to 15-20% of revenue.** This is management's own lever [MC] (CALL Jun 2026) and would lift contribution because spares carry no site-execution cost. It requires order inflow not currently in the book, where spares are at most 6.6% [E] from [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

**Backward integration converting job work into in-house throughput.** Rs 2.35 cr of job work charges plus faster cycle times is the stated prize: 'what this facility is going to do is going to improve our throughput. We are going to be able to actually ramp up the delivery cycles and hopefully be able to compress the working days even further' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.48).

**Operating leverage on a fixed cost base that has stopped growing.** Management's commitment: 'Going forward, we look that new hiring will be at a very moderate level. Employee cost increase in employee cost will not be as much as increase in revenue' and likewise for other expenses [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Testable directly at the H1 FY27 result [AI].

**Repeat orders on type-tested capacities.** Each repeat avoids the design-approval and type-testing cost that crushed H1 FY26 - testing and calibration charges alone rose from Rs 0.24 cr to Rs 2.20 cr [F] (AR2026 p.48). The four-of-six AC plant capacities and all ATU/AFU capacities already tested are the asset here [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**Collection of the GST input credit.** Rs 8.35 cr sits in balances with government authorities because inputs bear 18% GST and warship supplies attract 5% [F] (AR2026 p.47); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Recovery is a one-off cash release, not a margin improvement [AI].

**Recognition of the Maharashtra PSI capital subsidy.** Worth Rs 9.8-12.2 cr on FY26 capex if management's 40-50% claim holds [E], and stated by the CMD to go 'directly into the bottom line' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Nothing is recognised today [F] (AR2026 p.38).
**What would NOT improve it:** price. There is no mechanism. Awards are to the lowest bidder and contracts carry no escalation clause [F] (RATING).
Our statements data provides six years of annual history (FY21-FY26), not ten [F] (NUMBERS). There is no pre-FY21 record in our evidence set.
FY22 cash-flow data - operating, investing, financing and free cash flow - is missing entirely, so the five-year cumulative cash-conversion and free-cash-flow measures are null [F] (NUMBERS).
Earnings per share is only available from FY25 onwards [F] (NUMBERS); pre-IPO share counts make earlier EPS uninformative anyway [AI].

**The 'quarterly' series is not quarterly.** It contains four columns - Sep 2024, Mar 2025, Sep 2025, Mar 2026 - which are half-years, because the company reports half-yearly [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Half-on-half comparisons in a business with 67% H2 revenue concentration are close to meaningless taken singly [AI].
Year-on-year sales and PAT growth fields in the half-yearly series are null, as is the one-year promoter-holding change - the latter because the company listed only in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS).

Our statements data is stated on a consolidated basis [F] (NUMBERS), but the subsidiary is immaterial (nil turnover, Rs 2.23 cr of assets) so the consolidated and standalone series are near-identical [F] (AR2026 p.29).

The audited accounts are prepared under Indian GAAP / Accounting Standards notified under Section 133, not Ind AS [F] (AR2026 p.40). Several presentation choices below follow from that, including the capitalisation of deferred revenue expenditure, which would not be permitted under Ind AS [AI].
Shareholding data is available for only two dates - September 2025 and March 2026 [F] (NUMBERS) - because the company listed in August 2025.

**Revenue growth is real and audited.** Rs 98.73 cr to Rs 153.55 cr, +55.5%, identical in the standalone and consolidated accounts [F] (AR2026 p.24). Gross sales before GST were Rs 172.09 cr, of which sale of product Rs 169.18 cr, sale of services Rs 2.86 cr and other operating revenue Rs 0.05 cr [F] (AR2026 p.48).

**Profit growth is flattered below the operating line.** PBT rose 32.8% (Rs 18.69 cr to Rs 24.82 cr) while PAT rose 64.7% (Rs 13.00 cr to Rs 21.40 cr) [F] (AR2026 p.38). The whole of that gap is tax [E].

**The tax rate is the single largest unexplained item in the accounts.** Total tax expense fell from Rs 5.69 cr to Rs 3.41 cr on higher profit - an effective rate of 13.76% versus 30.4% [F] (AR2026 p.38). Current tax was Rs 3.98 cr (16.1% of PBT), plus Rs 0.42 cr of short provision for prior periods, less a deferred tax credit of Rs 0.99 cr. **No document in our evidence set explains why** [F - absence of disclosure]. Our statements data flags it amber [F] (NUMBERS). Normalising to FY25's rate would cut FY26 PAT by about Rs 4.1 cr [E].

**Other income is small but rising and non-operating.** Rs 1.51 cr versus Rs 0.36 cr, of which interest income Rs 1.40 cr on IPO cash [F] (AR2026 p.48). It was 8.0% of PBT in FY26 against 0.0% in FY25 [F] (NUMBERS).

**Depreciation contains a non-standard item.** Of Rs 5.78 cr, only Rs 2.60 cr is depreciation on tangible assets and Rs 0.20 cr amortisation of software; **Rs 2.98 cr is 'Amortization on Deferred revenue expenditure'** [F] (AR2026 p.48) - the capitalised P17A project costs and share-issue expenses discussed under accounting quality. That item is now fully amortised [F] (AR2026 p.41).

**Buildings are depreciated over 60 years against Schedule II's 30 years** for non-factory buildings, on a management technical estimate [F] (AR2026 p.40). Depreciation is on the written-down-value method [F] (AR2026 p.40).

**Directors' remuneration is a visible and fast-growing charge**: Rs 3.46 cr within employee benefit expense, up from Rs 2.01 cr, +72% [F] (AR2026 p.48). The related-party note shows Rs 4.60 cr paid to key managerial personnel, up from Rs 2.86 cr [F] (AR2026 p.51) - the two figures differ and neither is reconciled to the other [AI].

**No exceptional or extraordinary items, no prior-period items and no other comprehensive income in FY26** [F] (AR2026 p.24, p.38). FY25 carried Rs 0.05 cr of prior period expenses [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

**No ESOP cost was recognised in FY26**, because 'the vesting of the options commences from April 2026' [F] (AR2026 p.41). 7,00,750 options are outstanding at an exercise price of Rs 2 [F] (AR2026 p.52).

**The balance sheet is a working-capital vehicle.** Of Rs 299.93 cr of standalone total assets, current assets are Rs 243.03 cr (81%), of which trade receivables Rs 105.43 cr, inventories Rs 54.77 cr, cash and equivalents Rs 57.51 cr and other current assets Rs 19.94 cr [F] (AR2026 p.38). Net tangible fixed assets are Rs 21.54 cr [F] (AR2026 p.38).

**Receivables are the dominant asset and they are almost entirely unprovided.** Gross Rs 105.78 cr against a provision for doubtful debts of Rs 0.35 cr - 0.33% [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.47). There are no disputed receivables and none considered doubtful in the ageing table [F] (AR2026 p.47). Given AAA-rated PSU shipyard counterparties, a low provision is defensible [AI]; the level of the asset is the issue, not its quality.

**Receivables ageing improved sharply.** Over-six-month receivables fell from Rs 46.97 cr (49.3% of gross) to Rs 17.37 cr (16.5%) [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.47). Over-two-year receivables are Rs 0.17 cr. This is the strongest single piece of evidence for the working-capital improvement [AI].

**Inventory is Rs 54.77 cr, 18.3% of total assets, and is a key audit matter** [F] (AR2026 p.34, p.47). Composition: raw materials Rs 31.47 cr, work-in-progress Rs 22.85 cr, finished goods Rs 0.45 cr [F] (AR2026 p.47). WIP fell slightly year on year while raw materials rose 38.7% [F] (AR2026 p.47) - consistent either with pre-buying against commodity inflation or with a build for H1 FY27 deliveries [AI].

**Other current assets rose 123%, from Rs 8.94 cr to Rs 19.94 cr**, driven by advances to suppliers (Rs 3.22 cr to Rs 10.65 cr) and balances with government authorities (Rs 2.30 cr to Rs 8.35 cr) [F] (AR2026 p.47). An analyst raised this directly; the CFO attributed it to supplier advances and blocked GST input credit [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**Non-current investments of Rs 16.02 cr are largely non-operating**: mutual funds Rs 9.26 cr, investment property (residential Rs 2.50 cr and commercial Rs 2.10 cr), the Trezor investment Rs 1.67 cr, key-person insurance Rs 0.17 cr, fixed deposits over 12 months Rs 0.31 cr and co-operative bank shares [F] (AR2026 p.46). Plus current investments of Rs 5.15 cr [F] (AR2026 p.38).

**Debt is down and re-priced.** Total borrowings Rs 39.46 cr standalone (Rs 37.46 cr consolidated), of which short-term Rs 33.55 cr - cash credit from SBI Rs 25.01 cr at 8.75% and Yes Bank Rs 3.98 cr at 8.50%, SBI GECL Rs 3.00 cr at 8.65%, plus current maturities Rs 1.56 cr [F] (AR2026 p.38, p.43). **The entire unsecured NBFC book at 15.00-18.50% - nine loans from Poonawalla, Bajaj, Neo Growth, TATA Capital, Protium, IIFL, MAS, Kisetsu Saison, FedBank, Unity, Axis and Standard Chartered - was cleared to nil** [F] (AR2026 p.44). Debt-equity fell from 0.40x to 0.18x [F] (AR2026 p.53).

**Cash rose from Rs 5.93 cr to Rs 57.51 cr**, of which Rs 52.89 cr is investments with original maturity under three months [F] (AR2026 p.48) - essentially the unspent portion of the IPO proceeds rotating through liquid instruments [AI].

**Equity is Rs 219.63 cr standalone / Rs 215.86 cr consolidated**, of which securities premium Rs 160.54 cr and retained earnings Rs 51.96 cr [F] (AR2026 p.38, p.43, p.56). Share capital is Rs 7.13 cr - 3,56,30,409 shares of Rs 2 [F] (AR2026 p.42).
**Advances from customers rose from Rs 0.12 cr to Rs 9.48 cr** within other current liabilities [F] (AR2026 p.44) - a favourable working-capital development that management did not highlight [AI].

sections.title: Working capital - the central operating question

subsections.title: Why the headline number misleads on its own

blocks.text: The headline everyone quotes is 'working capital cycle improved from ~570 days (FY25) to ~370 days (FY26)' [F] (PPT Aug 2026). It appears on the second slide of the presentation and was the first thing two analysts congratulated management on [F] (CALL Jun 2026). It is misleading taken alone, for four reasons.

items: **It is a year-end ratio measured against a year in which two-thirds of revenue landed in the second half.** H1 FY26 revenue was Rs 50.72 cr and H2 was roughly Rs 102.8 cr [F] (RATING); [E]. Any days-based ratio computed on closing balances divided by full-year revenue improves mechanically when revenue is back-loaded, because the denominator includes six months of sales that had barely been invoiced when the receivable book was struck [AI].

**The FY25 base of 570 days is disputed by the company's own rating agency, which computed 378 days for the same year** [F] (RATING). If 378 is the right base, the improvement is roughly nil rather than 200 days. The two figures have never been reconciled in any document [F].

**Our statements data gives a third set of numbers**: working-capital days of 343 in FY25 falling to 253 in FY26, and a cash conversion cycle of 583 days falling to 377 [F] (NUMBERS). The 377 happens to be close to the company's 370, but it is built from different components [AI].

**Net capital turnover - revenue per rupee of working capital - actually deteriorated, from 1.27x to 1.13x** [F] (AR2026 p.53). That is the company's own audited ratio, disclosed in the same annual report as the 570-to-370 claim, and it points the other way [AI].

blocks.text: The improvement is real but smaller and differently caused than presented. The defensible evidence is the receivables ageing, not the days ratio: over-six-month receivables fell from Rs 46.97 cr (49.3% of gross) to Rs 17.37 cr (16.5%) [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.47). That is a genuine collection improvement that a revenue-timing artefact could not produce.

blocks.text: Management's answer to the funding question is explicit and should be recorded as guidance: 'whatever the new working capital requirement will be funded by internal accruals and bank funding. If you look at our balance sheet, the balance sheet is not leveraged. And we can easily raise the required funds for working capital' [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Separately, in November 2025: 'once we cross the threshold limit of a 500 plus crores, we will not need any more capital raise from the market' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

Read those two statements together and the implication is uncomfortable: management contemplates no further equity raise **above** Rs 500 cr of revenue, which by construction leaves the path from Rs 154 cr to Rs 500 cr to be funded by debt and accruals. At a 370-day cycle that path requires roughly Rs 350 cr of incremental working capital [E], against rated bank limits of about Rs 90 cr [F] (RATING) and a sub-investment-grade credit rating [AI].

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

items: **1. Does the approval barrier survive the policy that created it?** The registrations are valuable because few firms hold them. But the same Atmanirbhar Bharat programme that gave SRL its opening is explicitly designed to multiply qualified domestic suppliers - more than 4,600 items under indigenisation initiatives, 'policy reforms, simplified procurement procedures, and higher localisation targets... enabling private players to become an integral part of India's defence supply chain' [F] (AR2026 p.22). A scorecard measures the barrier today; it cannot price the government's intention to lower it [AI].

**2. Can a moat that does not touch price ever produce excess returns?** SRL's moat governs who may bid. It does not govern what the winning bid earns, because the buyer runs a lowest-bidder tender with no escalation clause [F] (RATING). Return on capital employed fell from 17.43% to 12.23% while the company was reportedly holding 64% share [F] (AR2026 p.23, p.53); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). If a 64% share in a protected niche produces a 12% return on capital against a 15% cost of equity in our model [F] (NUMBERS), the moat is protecting a business that does not currently earn its cost of capital - and no scorecard can tell us whether scale eventually fixes that or whether the buyer simply captures the benefit [AI].

blocks.text: **SRL has a real moat, and it is the wrong kind of moat to justify the current price** [AI]. It is a qualification moat: multi-year, non-purchasable, administered by the customer, and worth a great deal in win rate and in aftermarket annuity. The evidence for it is unusually good for a company this small - documented registrations across three directorates, a fifteen-platform delivery record, a five-year gestation the founder describes openly, and a test infrastructure that the Navy itself uses [F] (AR2026 p.22, p.15); [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

But the moat has three hard limits. It does not confer pricing power, because the award mechanism is a lowest-bidder tender on fixed-price terms [F] (RATING). It does not extend to the two growth vectors management emphasises - non-defence marine (where foreign owners specify local-presence vendors SRL does not have) and data centres (where the approval belongs to Smardt) [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). And it is being actively eroded by the policy that created it [F] (AR2026 p.22). A 4.6 average, with the strength concentrated in approvals and relationships, is consistent with a durable niche business earning a modest return on capital - which is what the 12.23% ROCE shows [F] (AR2026 p.23) - rather than with a compounder [AI].

The honest bull rebuttal: the aftermarket annuity is the part of the moat that is least visible in today's numbers and most valuable over a decade. Spares and AMC on fifteen platforms, replenished every three to five years, at a claimed near-100% retention rate, is a real annuity that has been suppressed to 7% of revenue by the timing of the equipment cycle [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). If it returns to 15-20% of revenue, both the margin and the moat score improve materially [AI].

blocks.text: **The single most revealing line in the model is the present value of the explicit five-year period: Rs 48.0 cr in the bear case, Rs 25.9 cr in the base case and Rs 1.6 cr in the bull case** [F] (NUMBERS). Faster growth destroys near-term value in this business, because at these working-capital intensities every incremental rupee of revenue absorbs more cash than it generates. In the bull case, 99.6% of the enterprise value is terminal value [E]. That is not a modelling quirk - it is the honest mathematical expression of a 250-to-370-day cash conversion cycle [AI].

We do not assign numerical probabilities; the evidence does not support that precision, and false precision on a company with one year of listed disclosure and half-yearly reporting would be misleading [AI]. Qualitatively:

items: **The bear case's growth assumption (12% starting, fading to 5%) looks too pessimistic against the evidence.** The company has a Rs 271 cr opening order book against Rs 154 cr of revenue, four of eight ongoing projects completing in FY27, and programmes such as FPV (2 of 14 shipsets) and NGOPV (3 of 7) that are barely started [F] (AR2026 p.7); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [F] (PPT Aug 2026). Twelve per cent growth would require an order-execution failure, not merely a slowdown [AI].

**The bear case's margin assumption (23.0%) looks about right or even generous.** FY26 actual was 21.4%, and management guides 20-24% with commodity inflation acknowledged [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).
**The base case's margin assumption (27.0%) looks too optimistic.** It exceeds the top of management's own guidance and has not been achieved since FY25 [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**The base case's growth assumption (30% fading to 10%, a 19.8% five-year compound rate) looks reasonable to slightly conservative versus guidance** of ~40%, and reasonable to slightly aggressive versus the order-book evidence, given H2 FY26 book-to-bill of approximately 0.46x [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [E].

**The bull case requires everything to go right simultaneously**: 43.5% starting growth (above guidance), a 29.0% EBITDA margin (not achieved since FY24), and a fade only to 13% - while the model still shows negative free cash flow in years one through three [F] (NUMBERS).

**Our judgement:** a blend of the base case's growth and the bear case's margin is the most defensible reading of the evidence, which would sit between Rs 38.2 and Rs 72.5 per share - and closer to the lower half of that range [AI]. **All of these outcomes are far below the current price of Rs 375** [F] (NUMBERS).

subsections.title: Interpreting the DCF and its assumptions

items: **Every scenario in the model values the equity far below the market price:** bear Rs 38.2 (-89.8%), base Rs 72.5 (-80.7%), bull Rs 106.9 (-71.5%) [F] (NUMBERS). The entire sensitivity grid runs Rs 55.4 to Rs 101.6 [F] (NUMBERS).

**The model's assumptions are not hostile.** The base case uses a 27.0% EBITDA margin - above the FY26 actual of 21.4% and above the top of management's guided range; a 25.2% tax rate rather than the FY26 effective rate; a 272.7-day working-capital assumption better than the company's stated 370-day cycle; and a 15.0% cost of equity with a beta of 1.15 for a BSE-SME small cap [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**The starting growth rate is capped at 30%** by the model's own rule, which is below management's ~40% guidance [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (PPT Aug 2026). The bull case at 43.5% starting growth is the scenario that exceeds guidance, and it still values the equity at Rs 106.9.

**The model's structural insight is the working-capital charge.** Base-case free cash flow is negative in years one and two even at a materially improved working-capital assumption [F] (NUMBERS). This is the mathematical statement of the forensic finding that five years of accounting profit produced negative cumulative operating cash [E].

**The reliance on terminal value is extreme**: 91% of base-case enterprise value and 99.6% in the bull case [E] from [F] (NUMBERS). Investors should understand they are being asked to pay for cash flows beyond FY31, in a business whose current business line is under ten years old [AI].

**What would legitimately move the DCF output up:** a sustained fall in working-capital days (the single biggest lever), a margin recovery driven by the spares mix, recognition of the Maharashtra PSI capital subsidy, or a lower cost of equity following main-board migration and improved disclosure [AI].

**What the DCF cannot capture:** option value on data centres, exports and non-defence marine, none of which is in any scenario [F] (NUMBERS); and the value of the approval moat beyond the terminal growth rate [AI].

blocks.text: **What 83.8% compounding for five years means in rupees.** Applied to the Rs 154 cr base, it implies revenue of roughly Rs 3,250 cr by year five [E] - against a stated capacity ceiling of Rs 400 cr from existing infrastructure [MC] (CALL Jun 2026), a total addressable market that management sizes at Rs 3,000-3,500 cr over 2-2.5 years for the entire industry [MC] (CALL Jun 2026), and a Rs 271 cr order book [F] (AR2026 p.7). **The price requires SRL to capture, within five years, roughly the whole of the market its own management describes** [AI].

**The key forensic conclusion.** The rule-based screen flags this directly as a red item: 'Price needs growth well above trend - today's price implies about 84% a year sales growth for five years, against 20% in the base case' [F] (NUMBERS). The price does not merely assume management delivers its guidance. It assumes management delivers roughly twice its most aggressive public aspiration, at a margin above its guided range, for five consecutive years - in a business that has never funded its own growth from operating cash flow [AI].
A reverse DCF is a statement about one model's assumptions, not a proof. The honest case against the conclusion above rests on five points, and they deserve to be stated at full strength [AI]:

items: **1. The model's discount rate may be too high for the asset.** A 15.0% cost of equity with a 1.15 beta is applied to a supplier whose customers are AAA-rated defence PSUs and the Government of India, with essentially no credit risk, no disputed receivables and a 0.33% doubtful-debt provision that has never proved inadequate [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (AR2026 p.47). A defence-qualified supplier with government counterparties arguably deserves a lower equity risk premium than a generic small-cap industrial. At a 13.3% WACC the base-case value rises to Rs 93.6 [F] (NUMBERS) - still far below the price, but the direction matters [AI].

**2. A five-year explicit period is short for a business whose revenue arrives on twenty-year platform cycles.** A warship class delivers shipsets over a decade and spares for decades after. The model's terminal growth of 5.5% may understate the annuity attached to fifteen already-delivered platforms plus the FPV, NGOPV and FSS programmes barely begun [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [AI].

**3. The model penalises exactly the thing the company is fixing.** Base-case free cash flow is negative in years one and two purely because of the working-capital charge [F] (NUMBERS). The company took its stated cycle from ~570 to ~370 days in one year and cut over-six-month receivables from 49.3% to 16.5% of the book [MC] (PPT Aug 2026); [E]. If the cycle continues to compress, the near-term cash drag reverses and the explicit-period present value rises sharply [AI].

**4. The model contains no option value.** Data centres, exports, non-defence marine, the Maharashtra PSI capital subsidy (potentially Rs 9.8-12.2 cr on FY26 capex alone), and the Danfoss service franchise are all excluded [F] (NUMBERS); [E]. Each is currently unevidenced, but a company with a genuine qualification moat in one niche has non-zero probability of extending it [AI].

**5. The base rate for this kind of screen is imperfect.** Reverse DCFs have flagged many high-multiple Indian defence and capital-goods names as unjustifiable through periods in which they compounded earnings faster than any model allowed, because the models cap growth (this one caps the starting rate at 30%) while order-driven businesses in a policy upcycle do not [F] (NUMBERS); [AI].

**Where the counter-argument runs out:** it can close a gap of 20-40%. It cannot close a gap of 71.5% to the bull case, and none of the five points changes the fact that the company has produced negative cumulative operating cash flow over five years, that its order book fell 17% in the most recent half, or that its highest-margin revenue line is at most 6.6% of the forward book [E]; [F] (NUMBERS).

blocks.text: **This is not a rating and does not translate into one.** It is a diagnostic: it says the operating asset is respectable (visibility 6, moat 6, capacity 6, balance sheet 8) and that the price and the governance are where the problems sit. Note also that scores 13 and 14 are entirely a function of the model in front of us - if you disagree with the DCF, you should disagree with the average [AI].

Shree Refrigerations occupies a genuinely defensible position in a structurally growing niche. It holds registrations from all three Indian naval professional directorates - marine engineering for AC and refrigeration plants, naval architecture for HVAC, and electrical engineering for control panels - plus DQA-Warship Projects approval, and claims to be the only Indian firm registered across all three [F] (AR2026 p.22); [MC] (PPT Aug 2026). Those registrations took the company five years to earn, cannot be bought, and are becoming more valuable as shipyards shift from component-wise to turnkey ordering - a shift corroborated by turnkey HVAC being 59% of the order book [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

The delivery record behind that position is unusually concrete for a company this size: fifteen named platforms with shipset counts, including the P17A Nilgiri-class frigates, the Scorpene submarine INS Vagsheer, the Fleet Support Ships and the Next Generation Offshore Patrol Vessels, and two ships commissioned by the Prime Minister carrying SRL plant [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.12). Behind that sits a test infrastructure - a 300 TR chiller bed, a marine tilt rig, a controlled-ambient AC room the Navy itself uses - that management credibly claims is unique in India [F] (AR2026 p.15); [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

FY26 delivered on what was promised: revenue of Rs 153.55 cr against guidance of Rs 140-150 cr, a PAT margin of 13.9% against 13-14% guided, capex of Rs 24.38 cr against Rs 25 cr guided, and the new plant commissioned on schedule on 20 June 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.24, p.25); [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). The IPO repaired the balance sheet properly - gearing from 0.40x to 0.18x, the entire 15-18.5% NBFC borrowing stack cleared to nil, interest cover to 7.2x and net cash on the balance sheet [F] (AR2026 p.44, p.53). Operating cash flow turned positive for the first time in the disclosed record, and receivables older than six months fell from 49.3% to 16.5% of the book [F] (AR2026 p.39); [E]. An order book of Rs 271 cr opens FY27, against a policy backdrop of over 75% domestic sourcing in defence modernisation [F] (AR2026 p.7, p.20).

And there is a real annuity underneath, currently suppressed. Spares and AMC on fifteen delivered platforms, replenished every three to five years, at a claimed near-100% retrofit retention rate, with service teams already positioned in five port cities [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.14). That business fell to 7% of revenue in FY26 because of where the equipment cycle sits. If it returns toward the 15-20% management targets, both the margin and the cash cycle improve materially [AI].

The price is the first and largest problem. At Rs 375 the equity trades at 61x trailing earnings, 41.8x EV/EBITDA, 8.95x EV/sales and 6.19x book, and **every scenario in our DCF values it far below - bear Rs 38.2, base Rs 72.5, bull Rs 106.9** [F] (NUMBERS). The reverse DCF puts the implied requirement at about 84% annual sales growth for five years against a base-case equivalent of 19.8% [F] (NUMBERS). Management's own most aggressive public aspiration - Rs 1,000 cr by FY30-31 - implies roughly 45.5% compound growth [E], barely half what the price demands.

The second problem is cash. Across the five years for which operating cash flow is disclosed, the company has reported roughly Rs 53 cr of profit and consumed roughly Rs 29 cr of operating cash [E] from [F] (NUMBERS). Three-year CFO/PAT is -0.34x, three-year free cash flow is -Rs 51 cr, and free cash flow was still negative in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). At the 370-day cycle management quotes, a single year of 40% growth would absorb roughly Rs 62 cr of incremental working capital against Rs 57.5 cr of cash [E].

The third is that the growth evidence is deteriorating exactly where it matters. The order book fell from Rs 327.57 cr at 30 September 2025 to Rs 270.8 cr at 31 March 2026 - a 17% decline implying an H2 book-to-bill of approximately 0.46x [F] (RATING); [F] (AR2026 p.22); [E]. Neither the CMD's letter, nor the MD&A, nor the investor presentation mentions it; all three lead with the 1.8x coverage ratio instead [F] (AR2026 p.7, p.12, p.22); [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

The fourth is governance. Managerial remuneration breached Section 197 in a year of record reported profit, the company told shareholders its Section 198 profits were 'inadequate', four AGM resolutions were required to ratify the breach and pre-authorise FY27, and the overall ceiling has been raised from 11% to 15% of net profits with up to Rs 5 cr payable even in a year of no profits [F] (AR2026 p.32, p.77, p.72, p.79). Four of five executive directors are one family. A residential flat was bought from the promoters with the title deed still in their names; vehicles were bought from KMP; and a Rs 5.69 cr intra-group land purchase has left an unexplained Rs 4.30 cr permanent consolidation adjustment [F] (AR2026 p.51, p.35, p.38, p.56).

The fifth is that the second growth engine does not exist yet. The data-centre agreement is non-exclusive, signed by a subsidiary with zero turnover whose only asset of substance is a deposit placed with its own parent, with no orders - 'we have an enquiry book' - no manufacturing, and revenue explicitly excluded from FY27 guidance [F] (AR2026 p.24, p.29, p.51); [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

subsections.title: Where the price sits against the evidence

blocks.text: Shree Refrigerations is a real business with a real, narrow moat, trading at a price that our valuation work cannot support under any scenario examined. At Rs 375 the equity sits 71.5% above the bull-case fair value of Rs 106.9, 80.7% above the base case of Rs 72.5, and 89.8% above the bear case of Rs 38.2 [F] (NUMBERS). The entire sensitivity grid - nine combinations of WACC and terminal growth - runs from Rs 55.4 to Rs 101.6 [F] (NUMBERS). The reverse DCF frames the same conclusion from the other side: the price requires about 84% annual sales growth for five years, against 19.8% in the base case and roughly 45.5% implied by management's own most aggressive aspiration [F] (NUMBERS); [E]. **We express no rating and no price target; we report where the model sits against the price and why** [AI].

**What drives the gap.** Four things, in order of magnitude. First, the model's working-capital assumption of 272.7 days makes growth cash-destructive for the first two years, so the explicit five-year period contributes only Rs 25.9 cr of the Rs 296.4 cr base-case enterprise value - 91% is terminal value, and 99.6% in the bull case [F] (NUMBERS); [E]. Second, the starting growth rate is capped at 30% by the model's own rule, below management's ~40% guidance [F] (NUMBERS). Third, the WACC of 14.8% on a beta of 1.15 is applied to a business whose customers carry essentially no credit risk. Fourth - and pointing the other way - the base case assumes a 27.0% EBITDA margin, above the FY26 actual of 21.4% and above the top of management's guided band, so the model is generous on margin even as it is conservative on cash [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (PPT Aug 2026); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

The honest reading is that a reasonable investor could argue the first three inputs and close some of the gap. None of those arguments closes a 71.5% gap to the bull case, and none of them addresses the three forensic facts that sit outside the model: five years of cumulative negative operating cash flow against Rs 53 cr of cumulative profit; an order book that fell 17% in the half-year in which revenue doubled; and a statutory remuneration breach ratified retrospectively while the ceiling was being raised [E]; [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (RATING); [F] (AR2026 p.22, p.32, p.79).

subsections.title: Investment horizon and when to re-review

items: **Horizon.** This is not a company that can be assessed on a quarterly horizon, and management has said so explicitly - it reports half-yearly and argues that even annual reporting is more informative for its business [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Anyone underwriting the equity is underwriting a three-to-five-year naval order cycle, in a business whose cash converts over 250-370 days. A horizon shorter than three years is a bet on multiple expansion, not on the business [AI].

**Re-review trigger 1 - the H1 FY27 results and call, expected around November 2026.** The specific disclosures to test: the closing order book at 30 September 2026 against Rs 271 cr; H1 order inflow against the roughly Rs 47 cr implied H2 FY26 run rate; H1 revenue against roughly Rs 71 cr (H1 FY26 grown 40%); the EBITDA margin against the 20-24% band; whether the promised H1/H2 evening-out has occurred; the spares share of revenue against 7%; the working-capital cycle against 370 days; and whether the Rs 8.35 cr of blocked GST credit has come down as management stated it would in H1 [F] (AR2026 p.7, p.47); [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [E].

**Re-review trigger 2 - the FY27 annual report, expected around July-August 2027.** Test: whether customer concentration is disclosed for the first time; whether the Section 197 position is compliant; whether any further related-party asset purchases occurred; whether the Rs 4.30 cr consolidation adjustment is explained; whether the effective tax rate normalises; whether the Maharashtra PSI subsidy is recognised; whether ESOP cost appears now that vesting has begun; and whether promoter pledge disclosure is provided [F] (AR2026 p.32, p.38, p.41, p.51, p.56).

**Re-review trigger 3 - the next CARE rating action, due around December 2026.** The positive trigger on scale is met; the sub-200-day operating-cycle trigger is not. An upgrade would be meaningful third-party validation; a negative action on the 360-day cycle trigger would be a serious warning [F] (RATING).
**Re-review trigger 4 - any Regulation 30 announcement** of a material order, an equity raise, a promoter pledge, a data-centre contract, or a change in the executive board [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS).

**Re-review trigger 5 - main-board migration**, which management expects to become possible from roughly FY28 and which would bring quarterly reporting and full corporate-governance disclosure [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

**What would make us rebuild the model from scratch:** a sustained working-capital cycle below 250 days, because that is the single input that turns this from a cash-consuming into a cash-generating business and it is the assumption doing most of the damage in the DCF [F] (NUMBERS); [AI].

blocks.text: For balance, the conclusion that would change our view fastest is not a valuation argument but an operating one: a closing order book above Rs 350 cr at 30 September 2026, combined with a spares share above 12% of revenue. That combination would simultaneously restore the growth evidence and validate the margin-recovery case, and it is testable within two months of this report [AI].

**This is initial coverage.** No previous report from this dashboard was available in our evidence set, so there is no prior set of numbers, guidance items, risks or thesis positions to test this report against. The only prior internal material available is a set of earlier desk notes, which flagged the same core concerns we reach independently here - EBITDA margin compression from 27.3% to 21.4% with management expecting further commodity pressure; a working-capital cycle still at 370 days after improving from 570; the collapse of spares and services from 30% of revenue to 7%; heavy H2 revenue weighting making any single half unrepresentative; a 40% CAGR guidance described as 'unusually aggressive for a Rs 153 cr revenue base'; and an unconfirmed promoter pledge position [AI] (BOARD). Spares and services as a share of revenue against 7% in FY26 and a 15-20% target - the entire margin-recovery case rests on it, and the order book contains at most 6.6% spares and services [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [E] from [F] (PPT Aug 2026).

The working-capital cycle and the Rs 8.35 cr of blocked GST input credit, which the CFO said 'will definitely come down in the first half of this year' - a dated, directly testable claim; plus whether CARE's sub-200-day operating-cycle positive trigger moves any closer [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.47); [F] (RATING).

Governance and supply: whether Section 197 compliance is restored, whether any promoter pledge is disclosed, whether further related-party asset purchases occur, and whether the Maharashtra Defence and Aerospace Venture Fund continues selling from its remaining 5.03% after cutting from 17.09% [F] (AR2026 p.42, p.32, p.51, p.79).
guidance: Revenue growth: 'CAGR ~40% for next 3 to 5 years (on the base of FY26)' - [MC] (PPT Aug 2026); reaffirmed on the call as 'we will continue to grow 40% CAGR rate for three to five years easily without much of an issue' and, when asked for the growth vision, simply 'CAGR 40%' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).
FY27 guidance excludes data centre: 'there will not be any revenue which we have considered from our data centre in FY27. So, our guidance for FY27 is without data centre' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

EBITDA margin: 'for next going forward, we expect that our EBITDA margin will remain somewhere between 20% to 24%', stated to be after considering commodity inflation - 'the commodity inflation has always been on an arc. And we did consider that before making this kind of guidance figure' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). This widens the earlier 'somewhere between 20% to 22%' - [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

Commodity impact on margin: 'the unprecedented commodity price rise which is happening right now, will have a small impact on us. And that impact is seen in EBITDA margins also going forward' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Spares and services mix: 'Going forward, we expect that spares and service revenue will be incorporating 15% of the total revenue. This will help us to increase EBITDA margin in the upcoming period'; elsewhere 'we are continuously working on it to increase our spares and service revenue to 15% to 20%' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Order book: 'we still have 1.8 times of the revenue in our closing order book. We have INR270 crores of the order book in our hand... The money required for execution of these orders, plus capacity required, factory required, and team required is already in place. We are very confident that we will achieve the guidance that has been given by our CEO' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). The annual report states FY27 'has commenced operations with an order book exceeding Rs 271 Crore' - [F] (AR2026 p.7).

Order inflow / tender pipeline: 'what we see very clearly from a defence segment is approximately a INR1,000-odd crore worth of tender will be floated. How much we will win and how much we will lose, that will depend. Currently, our market share is 64%' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Capex: 'the total CapEx requirement for Phase 1 at Hanbarwadi location is INR25 crores. Most of the CapEx has been done and the plant will be up and running by June'; and 'we don't expect a major CapEx involvement for the next couple of years at least... a small CapEx will always come in as and when the business will grow' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Capacity / peak revenue: 'What is the peak revenue which we can generate out of our infrastructure? This data we have already given last time also. We are still seeing up to INR400 crore kind of revenue we can generate out of existing infrastructure' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Not reconciled with the earlier 'up to Rs 550 crores to Rs 600 crores. We will not need any further manufacturing capacity. Once we have 100,000 square feet of manufacturing capacity operational' - [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

New products / data centre: 'our goal is to create a reference installation in FY27. And we expect a major revenue coming in from a data centre in FY28'; and 'this year, we are looking for a reference kind of installation. So, no addition to the top line or bottom line. Data centre revenue will start trickling in from next year onward, FY28 and onward, not in FY27' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Danfoss Turbocor service partnership: 'we are not looking at very high revenue from this particular service agreement at this point in time. Because the total population of these compressors is somewhere around 1,200-1,300 odd. What this is, actually, is a strategic investment' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Fund-raising: 'whatever the new working capital requirement will be funded by internal accruals and bank funding. If you look at our balance sheet, the balance sheet is not leveraged. And we can easily raise the required funds for working capital' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026). Earlier: 'once we cross the threshold limit of a 500 plus crores, we will not need any more capital raise from the market' - [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

Working capital: no target given. Asked directly where the cycle goes from 370 days, the CEO answered 'let me assure you, the improvement will continue going on. Number, I will come back to you' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Cost control / operating leverage: 'Going forward, we look that new hiring will be at a very moderate level. Employee cost increase in employee cost will not be as much as increase in revenue'; and 'Going forward, we expect that other expenses will not increase at the rate the revenue is expected to increase' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Seasonality: 'Going forward in FY27, we see H1 and H2 will not be as skewed as it was in FY26. There will be a lot of stimulus which will come, H1 and H2. But still H2 will be a little bigger as compared to H1' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

GST input credit recovery: 'the GST amount is lying with the government. It will come down once we apply for the refund of input tax credit. It will definitely come down in the first half of this year' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Long-term target reaffirmed: on the Rs 1,000 cr revenue and Rs 120-130 cr PAT figures given in the November 2025 presentation, 'we will stand by the number which is what has been mentioned by us'; and 'If you grow it by exactly 40%, you will end up in doing INR833 crore. But that doesn't work in business, sir. So, as a management of this company, we definitely are standing by our word. INR1,000 crore is the ladder which we are here in next 5 years and it will happen, sir' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Exports: 'we do have plans, Sridhar, for entering the export market. Plans are at a nascent stage. There are certain discussions. I won't like to elaborate too much on it'; clarified as being in the marine segment rather than data centre - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Main board migration: 'if my memory serves me right, we are not allowed to go to the main board for another two years at least. Almost another two years. And we definitely plan to move to the main board as and when the window is available to us' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026).

Quarterly reporting declined: 'in our line of business, it might indicate incorrect conclusions to you. So for somebody in our line of business, in the defence ecosystem, a half yearly or actually even an annual reporting is more accurate than a quarterly reporting' - [MC] (CALL Jun 2026); later softened to 'Yes, noted... we take your feedback' after a second analyst raised it.

Dividend: no dividend recommended for FY26 'To strengthen the financial position of the Company' - [F] (AR2026 p.24); and 'Considering the company's future growth plans and capital requirements, the company does not intend to declare dividends in the near term and plans to reinvest its profits back into the business' - [F] (AR2026 p.52).

Maharashtra PSI capital subsidy (given in the prior call, not repeated this quarter, and not recognised in the FY26 accounts): 'the Government of Maharashtra is giving us a capital subsidy to the extent of 50% of the capital investment in plant and machinery, including land and building... the eligibility for the subsidy goes on increasing that is a period of 10 years. So there's a steady stream getting into the bottom line' - [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); the presentation states a '40%-50% subsidy on CAPEX under PSI scheme of Government of Maharashtra' - [MC] (PPT Aug 2026).
